d: Learn about domain-scoped user IDs and the User type for identifying players in your games.
h:
Refer to the DevForum announcement for latest information on domain-scoped user ID rollout and timelines.

Roblox assigns each user a unique domain-scoped user ID per game or app they interact with. This page explains how domain-scoped identification works and how to use the User type in your game code.

The following concepts are central to user identification:

Concept Description
**User** A persistent account on Roblox.
**Player** The representation of a user within a running game's data model (see [Players](#/docs/players)).
User data type A data type that represents a user's identity within a specific domain. This is the standard identifier for referencing users in game code.
**Domain-scoped user ID** A numeric identifier that uniquely identifies a user within a specific [domain](#domain-scoped-user-ids). This identifier is different in every game and app.

Domain-scoped user IDs

A domain-scoped user ID is a unique identifier assigned to a user within a specific game or app. Unlike a global user ID, a domain-scoped user ID is only meaningful within the domain that issued it, so the same user has a different domain-scoped user ID in each game or app they interact with. Players who joined your game before the scoped ID rollout keep their original global user ID in that game (see Returning players).

Domain types are represented by DomainType:

Domain type Scoped to Example
DomainType.EXPERIENCE A specific game (universe) A player's ID in your game
DomainType.OAUTH A specific OAuth application A user's ID in your external tool

How domain-scoped IDs work

When a player joins your game, they receive a domain-scoped user ID that is unique to that game. The same player joining a different game receives a different domain-scoped user ID. This means:

  • Domain-scoped user IDs are integers, similar to existing global user IDs.
  • A domain-scoped user ID does not collide with any existing global user ID.
  • The same numeric value may appear in different domains for different users. The unique key is the combination of domain type, domain ID, and domain-scoped user ID.

Example scenario

The following example demonstrates how different games reference the same user:

Scenario User context User ID seen by game
User connects to **Game A** Returning player (visited before scoped IDs) `123` (global ID, unchanged)
User connects to **Game B** First visit after scoped ID rollout `500789` (domain-scoped user ID for Game B)
User connects to **Game C** First visit after scoped ID rollout `302441` (domain-scoped user ID for Game C)

Returning players

If a player already joined your game before the scoped user ID rollout, they keep their original global user ID in that game. This ensures existing data store keys, leaderboards, and inventories continue to work without any changes.

Working with the User Type

User is the standard way to identify users in game code. A User value carries the domain-scoped user ID alongside the domain type and domain ID, so the identity context always travels with the identifier. For full API details, see the User reference.

Get a User from a Player

The primary way to obtain a User is from a connected Player via Player.User:

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    local user = player.User
    print("Domain user ID:", user.Id)
    print("Domain type:", user.DomainType)
    print("Domain ID:", user.DomainId)
end)

Construct a User from an ID

To create a User from a known user ID within the current game, use User.fromId():

local user = User.fromId(knownUserId)

Using User with engine APIs

Engine APIs that accept a user ID parameter also accept User values directly. Using User is recommended:

-- Both forms work:
BadgeService:AwardBadge(player.User, badgeId)    -- Recommended
BadgeService:AwardBadge(player.UserId, badgeId)

-- Both forms work:
local target = Players:GetPlayerByUserId(player.User) -- Recommended
local target = Players:GetPlayerByUserId(someUserId)

When a numeric user ID is passed to an engine API that accepts user IDs, it is automatically wrapped into a User internally.

Engine APIs that return user IDs

Engine APIs that return numeric user IDs continue to use the same field names and types. Each returned ID is either a global ID or a domain-scoped user ID depending on whether the user joined the game before or after the scoped ID rollout:

  • Returning players (first joined before scoped ID launch) — the API returns the user's global user ID.
  • New players (first join after scoped ID launch) — the API returns the user's domain-scoped user ID.

Both global and domain-scoped user IDs are standard integers that do not collide, so existing code that reads these numeric fields continues to work.

Storing user identity

For data store keys within a single game, use user.Id directly:

local key = ("player_%d"):format(player.User.Id)
PlayerDataStore:SetAsync(key, data)

For values that may be read by other systems or need full domain context, serialize the User with ToString():

local encoded = player.User:ToString()
SomeDataStore:SetAsync("support_ticket_user", encoded)

-- Later, restore from the string
local user = User.fromString(encoded)

For more details on serialization guarantees, see the User reference.

Best practices

  • Use Player.User as the standard identifier in new code.
  • Use ToString() and fromString() when persisting or transmitting a User value.
  • Do not use a numeric user ID from one domain to identify a user in another domain.

When to use User or Player

  • Use Player for in-server actions: character movement, GUI, teleport, chat, inventory.
  • Use User for identity that outlives a session: data stores, Open Cloud tools, cross-game references.

kid.simple: Every Roblox account has a number that identifies it, called a user ID. Roblox is changing things so that each game gets its own private ID number for each player, called a domain-scoped user ID. So the same player has one number in your game and a different number in someone else's game. This page shows how to use the `User` type in your scripts so your saves, badges, and leaderboards keep working.
kid.analogy: It is like a school giving you a student number. Your number at your school is different from your number at a summer camp, even though you are the same person. Each place only understands its own number.
keyPoints: A User is your Roblox account. A Player is that account while it is inside a running game server.
New players get a different ID number in every game, so an ID only makes sense inside the game that gave it out.
Players who joined your game before this change keep their old global ID in your game, so old saves still work.
Get a player's `User` value with `player.User`. It has `Id`, `DomainType`, and `DomainId`.
Engine functions that take a user ID, like `BadgeService:AwardBadge()`, also accept a `User` value, and Roblox recommends passing the `User`.
For data store keys inside one game, use `player.User.Id`. To save the full identity for other systems, use `user:ToString()` and later `User.fromString()`.
Use `Player` for things during the session (movement, GUI, chat) and `User` for identity that lasts (saves, cross-game references).
Never use an ID number from one game to find a player in a different game.

terms.user ID: A number that identifies a Roblox account. For example, a player might be `123` in one game.
terms.domain: The place an ID belongs to, such as one specific game or one outside app. An ID only means something inside its own domain.
terms.domain-scoped user ID: An ID number that only works inside one game or app. The same player could be `500789` in Game B and `302441` in Game C.
terms.global user ID: The older kind of ID that was the same in every game. Returning players keep this one in games they already played.
terms.Datatype: A built-in kind of value in Luau, like `Vector3` or `User`. It is a value, not an object you see in the Explorer.
terms.DomainType: An enum that says what kind of domain the ID belongs to: `EXPERIENCE` (a game) or `OAUTH` (an outside app).
terms.serialize: Turn a value into text so it can be saved or sent somewhere, then turned back later. `ToString()` serializes a `User`.
terms.collide: When two different things accidentally get the same number. Scoped IDs never collide with global IDs.
terms.session: One visit to a server, from when a player joins until they leave.

example.title: Print a player's IDs and make a save key
example.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
	-- The User value for this player in this game
	local user = player.User
	print(player.Name, "has ID", user.Id, "in this game")

	-- A data store key that only needs to work inside this game
	local key = ("player_%d"):format(user.Id)
	print("Save key:", key)

	-- Full identity as text, safe to store for other systems
	local encoded = user:ToString()
	print("Saved as text:", encoded)
end)
explain: When a player joins, `PlayerAdded` runs the function and hands it the `player`.
`player.User` gives you the `User` value for that player in your game.
`user.Id` is the number for that player in this game only. It builds a save key like `player_500789`.
`user:ToString()` turns the whole identity into text, which you can turn back with `User.fromString()` later.

watchOut: Do not copy a player's ID from your game and use it in another game or tool. The number will point to nobody, or to someone else.
Do not panic about old saves. Players who joined before the change keep their old ID in your game.
Use `ToString()` and `User.fromString()` when you save a full `User`, not your own homemade format.
